blocks.text: But those Talmudists are also gravely mistaken who will have שמן קיק, oleum kik [kik oil], taken from a bird, since it is κίκινον ἔλαιον [kikinon elaion], that is, oil pressed from the seeds of the plant which the Egyptians called KIKI` [kiki]. Many ancient writers mention it. Thus Herodotus, book 1, chapter 92, says that the marsh-dwelling Egyptians use an ointment ἀπὸ τῶν σιλλικυπρίων τοῦ καρποῦ, τὸ καλεῦσι μὲν Αἰγύπτιοι KIKI` [apo tōn sillikypriōn tou karpou, to kaleusi men Aigyptioi kiki], from the fruit of the syllicyprium, which the Egyptians call KIKI. And Strabo, book 17, in his description of Egypt: Καὶ τὸ KIKKI` (read KIKI`) καρπός τις σπειρόμενος ἐν ἀρούραις, ἐξ οὗ ἔλαιον ἀποθλίβεται [Kai to kikki … karpos tis speiromenos en arourais, ex hou elaion apothlibetai]. And KIKI is a certain fruit, sown in the fields, from which oil is pressed. And Dioscorides, book 4: KIKI`, ἢ κρότων [kiki, ē krotōn], etc. ἐξ οὗ ἀποθλίβεται τὸ λεγόμενον κίκινον ἔλαιον [ex hou apothlibetai to legomenon kikinon elaion]. And Pliny, book 15, chapter 7: Oil is also made from the CICI tree, abundant in Egypt. Hence Hesychius: Κίκη· φυτόν [Kikē· phyton]; but it should be corrected to Κικί [Kiki]. And this is the very kikajon קיקיון of Jonah, and the elcheroa الخروع [al-kharwaʿ] of the Arabs. This was already observed by Jerome nearly thirteen hundred years ago. For the gourd, or ivy (he says on Jonah) we read in the Hebrew קיקיון, which in the Syriac and Punic language is also called elkeroa. Accordingly, in the Coptic Lexicon ^{a)} the Egyptian word KOYKI` [kouki] kuki [III, 42] (for which I would write KIKI` [kiki]) is rendered in Arabic حب الخروع [ḥabb al-kharwaʿ], the seed of elcheroa or alcheroa. And in Abenbitar, in the chapter خروع [kharwaʿ] cheroa, the words of Dioscorides on κικὶ [kiki], ἐξ οὗ ἀποθλίβεται τὸ λεγόμενον κίκινον ἔλαιον [ex hou apothlibetai to legomenon kikinon elaion], are rendered in Arabic thus: ومنها يتعصر الدهن المسمي قيقي وهو دهن الخروع [wa-minhā yutaʿaṣṣar al-duhn al-musammī qīqī wa-huwa duhn al-kharwaʿ], And from it is pressed the oil which they call the oil KIKI, which is the oil ALCHEROA. Indeed there are even some among the Talmudists for whom kik, from which the oil comes, is the same as kikajon. The Talmud, in the place cited above: ריש לקיש אמר קיקיון דיונה אמר רבה בר בר חנה לדידי חזי לי קיקיון דיונה ולצלוליבה דמי, Resh Lakish said: It is the kikajon of Jonah. Rabba Bar son of Hana said: As for me, I have seen the kikajon of Jonah, and it is a plant resembling the selulibah. Indeed it is the same, if selulibah is truly the alcheroa الخروع [al-kharwaʿ] of the Arabs, as is found in the Responsa of the Geonim, that is, of the illustrious doctors, where seluliba is defined: אילן סרק יש במקומינו ועושה גרעינים ועושין מהן שמן ומין סממנין וכל מי שיש בו צנה הרבה שותה ממנו ושמו בלשון ערבי אלכרו״ע ושמנו קורין דהן כרוע, A barren tree growing in our lands, bearing seeds from which oil is made, and a kind of red colouring. And whoever is seized by a severe chill drinks of this oil. In Arabic it is called alcheroa, and its oil the oil cheroa. So Baal Aruch cites it. But in Kimchi's Commentaries, where this same passage is quoted, the words ומין סממנין, and a kind of red colouring, appear nowhere. [col. 294] I therefore suspect that they were either added from elsewhere or corrupted, and that in their place we should read ומין שמשומין, and a kind of sesame, so that seliluba, or alcheroa, is said to be among the kinds of sesame, an opinion held by some of the ancients. Pliny, book 15, chapter 7, on manufactured oil: Next is that made from the CICI tree, abundant in Egypt; some call it croton, others trixis (or rather sili, as Salmasius on Solinus would have it read), others wild sesame. The Supplement to Dioscorides: Κικὶ, ἢ κρότων, οἱ δὲ σήσαμον ἄγριον [Kiki, ē krotōn, hoi de sēsamon agrion]. The Arabic Pandectarius: CICI of Dioscorides, or wild sesame, etc., kerva in Arabic. It should also be noted that in Herodotus it is called τὰ σιλλικύπρια [ta sillikypria], in the Supplement to Dioscorides σεσελὶ κύπριον [seseli kyprion], and in Pliny sili, words which seem to allude to the barbarian seluliba ^{(3)}. But this in passing; now to the matter at hand.
